A **scam** is a trick that gets you to hand over money, information or access to your accounts **by your own action**. A pickpocket takes your purse. A scammer makes you open the purse yourself and give it away, often while smiling and saying thank you. That single difference explains almost everything about fraud: why it works, why it is hard to recover from, and why the best protection is a habit in your own head rather than a lock on your door.
A yellow warning triangle
Every scam has warning signs; this course trains you to see them before you act.

Because you did the transfer, typed the PIN or shared the code, the bank's records show a payment that **you authorised**. That is why recovery is slow and sometimes impossible. It is not because the bank does not care. It is because, to the system, the payment looks normal. Speed of reporting matters a lot, and you will learn exactly what to do in Module 4.
The three parts every scam needs

Thousands of scams exist, and new ones appear every month. The good news is that underneath, they are built from the same three parts. If you can spot the parts, you do not need to memorise every new trick.

Notice that part three is always the same few things: **money, a code, or your personal details**. A real offer can survive you slowing down and checking. A scam cannot. That is why pressure is always part of the package.
Scam, mistake or bad business?

Not every loss is a scam. If a trader sells you poor quality cloth, that is bad business, and you can complain or return it. If a bank charges a wrong fee, that is an error you can dispute. A scam is different: the person **planned to deceive you from the start** and usually disappears after payment. Telling these apart helps you choose the right next step and the right place to report.
Worked example: taking apart a "promo winner" message

For example, Ngozi, a fish seller in Port Harcourt, receives this SMS: "Congrats! Your line has won N250,000 in our anniversary promo. To claim, send N5,000 processing fee to 0123456789 within 2 hours. Do not share this message."
The story: she has won a cash prize from her network.
The pressure: two hours only, and keep it secret so nobody can warn her.
The payment: N5,000 "processing fee" to a personal account number.

Her check: she never entered a promo. Real prizes do not require the winner to pay first. She calls her network's official customer care line from the number printed on her SIM pack or the network's official website, not a number in the SMS.
Customer care confirms there is no such promo. Ngozi deletes the message and warns her women's group on WhatsApp. She lost nothing because she paused long enough to see all three parts.
Fraud is a crime in Nigeria

Nigerian law treats scams seriously. The nickname **"419"** comes from **Section 419 of the Criminal Code**, which deals with obtaining property by false pretences. The **Advance Fee Fraud and Other Fraud Related Offences Act 2006** covers advance fee schemes, and the **Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act 2015** covers crimes committed with computers and phones, including identity theft. Agencies such as the **Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC)** and the **Nigeria Police Force National Cybercrime Centre (NPF-NCCC)** investigate these crimes.
Why this matters to you

Knowing it is a crime removes the shame. You are not reporting your own foolishness. You are reporting a criminal who chose to deceive you, and your report can help stop the same person from targeting the next woman.
The mindset this course builds
**Pause:** any message that asks for money, a code or personal details gets a pause, no matter how urgent it sounds.
**Verify:** check through a channel you found yourself, such as the number on the back of your ATM card or the official app, never the link or number in the message.
**Talk:** tell one trusted person before you pay. Scammers hate witnesses.
**Report:** if something goes wrong, act fast and tell the right people.
You will see these four habits again and again in this course. By the end, they should feel as natural as checking that the gas is off before you leave the house.

Scammers are not magicians. They are students of human feeling. They know that when we are frightened, excited or in love, the part of the brain that weighs evidence goes quiet and the part that wants quick relief takes over. A good scam is designed to push you into that state and keep you there until you pay.

This is why the old saying "only foolish people fall for scams" is wrong. Doctors, bankers, pastors and professors have lost money to fraud. What they had in common was not low intelligence. It was a strong feeling at the wrong moment, and no pause.

Most scams combine two or three levers. A fake bank call uses **authority** plus **fear** plus **urgency**. An investment scheme uses **greed** plus **trust** (because your friend joined) plus **urgency** ("the next cycle starts Monday").

Why we fall: three thinking shortcuts
**Social proof:** "Everyone in my church group has joined, so it must be fine." Popularity is not proof. Ponzi schemes grow exactly because many people join early.
**Sunk cost:** "I have already paid N20,000 in fees, I can't stop now." Scammers keep asking for one more fee because they know you want to rescue what you already paid.
**Reciprocity:** "He was so kind and patient with me." Scammers invest weeks of kindness so that saying no feels rude.
Worked example: spotting the levers in a phone call

For example, Halima, a teacher in Kaduna, gets a call. The caller knows her name and her bank. He says, "Madam, I am from the fraud desk. Someone is trying to withdraw N180,000 from your account right now. To stop it, read me the code we just sent to your phone."
Authority: he claims to be from the bank's fraud desk.
Fear: N180,000 is about to disappear.
Urgency: "right now".
The real request: the one-time password (OTP) that has just arrived. That code is what would let him complete a transaction on her account.
Halima uses the cool-down rule: she says, "I will call the bank myself," hangs up, and calls the number on the back of her ATM card.
The bank confirms no one from the bank called her. The OTP was for a transfer the scammer was trying to make with her details. Because she did not read it out, the transfer failed.
The cool-down rule

You cannot stop feeling fear or excitement. You can stop acting on it immediately. The cool-down rule is simple: **when a message makes you feel a strong emotion and asks for money, a code or personal details, you stop and do not act for at least ten minutes**. During those minutes you do two things: check through your own channel and tell one trusted person.
Notice the feeling. Say to yourself, "I am scared" or "I am excited". Naming it weakens it.
End the conversation politely. "Let me call you back" is enough. A real bank or employer will accept that.
Check through a number or app you found yourself.
Talk to one trusted person before any payment.
A sentence to practise
Practise saying out loud: "I don't do money or codes on the phone. I will go to the bank myself." Having the words ready makes it much easier to use them when your heart is racing.
Scammers often get angry or push harder when you slow down. That reaction is itself a strong sign. Genuine organisations do not insult you for being careful.

Finally, remember that tiredness and distraction make every lever stronger. Many people who lose money say it happened late at night, in a crowded market, or while cooking with a child crying. If you are busy, the safest answer to any money request is "later". A real opportunity will still be there in the morning.

Scammers do not need to know you personally. Many send the same message to thousands of numbers and wait for a few replies. Others do their homework and contact you with your full name, your bank and even your recent purchase. Both kinds exist. Knowing how they find you helps you understand why a caller who "knows things" is not proof that he is genuine.
Where scammers get your details
**Your own posts:** birthdays, children's school names, travel plans, new car photos and business phone numbers posted publicly on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok or WhatsApp status.
**Business listings:** if you sell online, your name and number are public. That is normal for business, but it means you will be targeted.
**Leaked or sold data:** customer lists can be leaked or stolen. A caller knowing your name and bank does not prove he works at the bank.
**Lost or stolen phones and documents:** a lost phone with no screen lock opens your messages, contacts and banking apps.
**Shoulder surfing:** someone watching you type your PIN at a POS stand or ATM.
**Fake forms and links:** "Fill this form to get the grant" pages that collect your BVN, NIN and account details.

Common targets in our communities

**Older relatives** are often targeted with calls that pretend to be from the bank or a grandchild in trouble, because they are more likely to trust authority and less used to smartphone tricks. **Traders and POS operators** handle many transfers each day and are targeted with fake alerts. **Young people and graduates** are targeted with job and "online business" offers. **Diaspora relatives** are targeted with emergency stories about family at home.
Worked example: reducing what a scammer can learn
For example, Blessing sells shoes on Instagram from Ibadan. Her personal Facebook is public, showing her children's school uniform, her date of birth and her bank's branded debit card in a photo.
She changes her personal Facebook so only friends can see posts.
She deletes the photo showing her debit card and the one showing the school badge.
She keeps her business page public but uses a separate business number for it.
She hides her date of birth year on her profile.
She tells her mother, "No one from my bank will ever call you for codes. If anyone says I am in trouble, call me first."
A scammer looking at her pages now sees only business information. Her family has a simple rule that blocks the most common emergency trick.
"He knew my name and account number"

Account numbers are given out every day to receive payments. Your name and account number alone do not let anyone take money, and knowing them does not prove a caller works at your bank. What thieves need is your PIN, password, OTP or card details. Never give those to anyone.
Scams that come through people you know

Not every approach comes from a stranger. When a friend's WhatsApp or Facebook account is hacked, the scammer messages everyone in her contact list, writing in her style: "Please send me N30,000, I will refund tomorrow, my app is not working." Because the message comes from a trusted name, people pay without thinking. The fix is simple: before sending money to anyone who asks by message, **call them on their normal number and hear their voice**. If they do not pick up, wait. A real friend will understand.

Some schemes also spread through relatives and church or market groups, with the person recruiting you honestly believing it is genuine. Their sincerity does not make the scheme safe. You can respect the person and still check the scheme.
You cannot hide completely, especially if you run a business. The goal is to make yourself a harder target than the next person, and to make sure your family knows the same rules you do.

Red flags in money messages
Some red flags are specific to transfers, and traders should learn them by heart:
**The alert does not match your balance.** A real credit increases your balance in your bank app or USSD balance check. A fake alert is just a text message.
**The sender is a normal phone number.** Bank alerts usually come from the bank's name as sender. But sender names can also be faked, so the balance check is the real test.
**"I sent too much, please send back the balance."** Check your actual balance first. Often nothing was sent at all.
**Screenshots as proof.** A screenshot of a transfer is a picture, not money. It can be edited in seconds.
Worked example: running the two-minute check

For example, Amaka runs a provision shop in Onitsha. A customer buys goods worth N38,500 and shows a phone screen saying "Transfer successful". Amaka's phone then gets an SMS: "Credit Alert: N38,500.00".
Code or PIN requested? No.
Pay before you receive? No, but she is giving goods before confirming money.
Rushing? Yes: "Madam, quick, my bus is leaving."
She opens her banking app and checks her balance. It has not changed.
She politely says, "Please wait, my network is slow. I'll release the goods once it shows in my app."
After five minutes the balance still has not changed and the customer leaves without the goods. The SMS and screenshot were both fake. Amaka saved N38,500 by checking the app instead of the SMS.
Make it a shop rule
Write "Goods released after payment shows in our app" on a card by your till. Customers then see it as your rule, not as you accusing them, and genuine customers will happily wait.
Red flags in messages and links

Phishing is when a message tries to get you to click a link or open a file so that you type your details into a fake page. Fake pages often copy a bank's logo and colours perfectly. The clues are usually small: a web address that is slightly misspelt, an address that is not your bank's official site, a shortened link, or a message that starts "Dear Customer" instead of your name. The safest habit is not to judge the link at all: **do not click links in unexpected messages about your money**. Open your bank's app or type the address you already know.
Spelling and grammar mistakes in a message that claims to be official.
Attachments such as "invoice.apk" or files you were not expecting. On Android, an .apk file installs an app, which can give a criminal control of your phone.
Requests to install a screen-sharing or "support" app so that someone can "help" you.
When there are no obvious red flags

Clever scams sometimes look clean. If something important is happening with your money and you feel even a small doubt, treat the doubt itself as a red flag. Call the organisation using a number you found yourself, visit the branch, or ask someone you trust. Being slow and safe is always better than being fast and sorry.

The golden rule
Your bank will **never** call, SMS, email or WhatsApp you to ask for your PIN, password, OTP, full card details or BVN. Anyone who asks for these is a scammer, no matter how much they know about you.
The fake 'BVN update' and 'account blocked' scam

A typical message says: "Dear customer, your BVN has been suspended due to a CBN directive. Click the link to update within 24 hours or your account will be blocked." The link leads to a page that looks like your bank's, asking for your account number, BVN, card details and PIN. A call version has a polite "customer care agent" who talks you through "reactivation" and then asks you to read out the OTP that arrives.

What is really happening: while he talks to you, he is trying to log in to your account or add his phone as a new device. The bank sends **you** an OTP to approve it. When you read it out, you approve his access.
How an OTP call scam unfolds
Call: 'Account at risk'
Scammer starts transaction
Bank sends you OTP
You read OTP aloud
Money leaves account
The OTP you receive approves the scammer's action, which is why reading it out is the moment of loss.
Fake credit alerts

A fake alert is a text message designed to look like a bank credit notification. Fraudsters use them when buying goods, paying for services, or claiming they "sent too much". Sender names on SMS can be faked, so an alert that looks right is not proof. **The only proof is your balance**, checked in your bank app, internet banking or by USSD balance enquiry.
Fake POS reversals and 'wrong transfer' tricks

There are two common versions. In the first, someone pays at your POS or by transfer, then comes back saying the transaction failed and asks you to "reverse" it by sending money back, when in fact it never failed or never arrived. In the second, you get an alert or a call: "I mistakenly sent N50,000 to your account, please send it back to this other account." Sometimes a real credit did come in from a stolen account, and when you send money "back" to a different account you help the thief move stolen money.
Worked example: handling a 'wrong transfer' call

For example, Funke, a POS operator in Abeokuta, gets a call: "Madam, I mistakenly transferred N50,000 to your account. Please send it to my brother's account, 2034..., I need it urgently for hospital."
She does not argue. She opens her own app and checks her balance and transaction history.
Case A: nothing has arrived. She ends the call. It was a fake alert scam.
Case B: a real N50,000 credit is there from an unknown name. She does **not** send money to any account the caller gives.
She calls her bank on the official number and reports an unexpected credit, asking the bank to handle any reversal to the original sender through official channels.
She keeps a screenshot of the call log and the credit.
Either way, Funke does not send money on a caller's instructions. Reversals go through the bank, back to the original source, never to a 'brother's account'.
Reversals are the bank's job
If a genuine transfer was a mistake, the sender's bank can contact your bank. You do not need to transfer anything yourself because a stranger called you. Let the banks handle it.

Fraudsters may also pose as staff of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), the EFCC or the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC). These agencies do not phone individuals to collect fees, PINs or OTPs, and they do not threaten arrest unless you pay by transfer. Treat such calls exactly like fake bank calls: end the call and check through the agency's official website.
Never share PIN, OTP, password, full card details or BVN with anyone who contacts you.

Only your balance in the app proves money arrived, not an SMS or screenshot.
Mistaken transfers are reversed through the bank, never by sending money to a new account.

A **romance scam** is when a criminal builds a fake relationship online to win your trust and then asks for money. It hurts twice: you lose money and you lose someone you believed loved you. Romance scammers are patient. They may chat every day for weeks or months before asking for anything.
A broken red heart
Romance scams break hearts and bank balances, so learn the pattern before it starts.
Where they find people

Romance scammers use Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, dating apps, and even wrong-number WhatsApp messages ("Hello, is this Mrs Adeyemi? Sorry, wrong number. You have a beautiful profile picture..."). They often claim jobs that explain why they cannot meet: soldier on a foreign mission, engineer on an oil rig, doctor with an international aid agency, or a businessman travelling abroad.

Friendly first contact
Fast intense affection
Move to private chat
Crisis needs money
More fees and excuses
Romance scams follow a predictable path from charm to crisis to repeated requests.
Warning signs
**Love too fast:** strong declarations of love within days or a few weeks.
**Moves you off the platform quickly** to WhatsApp, Telegram or Google Chat, away from safety tools.
**Never available for a live video call.** Camera is always "broken", network is "poor", or they send pre-recorded videos.
**Photos look like a model or a professional shoot.** These are often stolen from someone else's profile.
**Stories that don't add up:** details change, time zones are wrong, or the accent does not match the claimed background.
**A crisis that needs money:** customs fees for a "parcel" of gifts, hospital bills, a flight ticket to visit you, a frozen bank account, or a legal fee.
**Requests for unusual payment:** gift cards, crypto, or transfers to a friend's account.
**Asks for intimate photos** and later threatens to share them unless you pay. This is called **sextortion**. Do not pay; report it.
Checks you can do
Ask for a live video call at a time you choose. A genuine person will manage one, even briefly.
Do a reverse image search of their profile photo using Google Lens (hold the photo, tap the Lens icon) to see if the picture appears under other names.
Search their name together with the words 'scam' or 'fraud'.
Never send money, gift cards or crypto to someone you have not met in person, however good the reason.
Tell a trusted friend about the relationship. Scammers push secrecy because outsiders see clearly.
Worked example: the 'parcel at customs' story

For example, Grace, a widow in Enugu, has chatted for two months with 'Richard', who says he is an engineer abroad. He sends her love songs every morning. One day he says he has shipped her a parcel with gifts and some cash, and a 'customs agent' then messages her asking for N350,000 to clear it at the airport.
Grace notices three red flags: they have never had a live video call, the payment is to a personal account, and the 'customs agent' only contacted her by WhatsApp.
She asks Richard for a live video call that evening. He says his camera is broken.
Her daughter helps her do a Google Lens search on his photo. The same face appears on a profile with a different name.
Grace stops replying, blocks both numbers, reports the profiles on the platform, and saves screenshots.
Grace loses no money. She feels sad and embarrassed, and her daughter reminds her that these criminals are skilled professionals who target kind people. That is not a flaw in her.
If a friend is in one

Do not say "How could you be so foolish?" Shame pushes people back to the scammer, who is always kind. Instead, ask gentle questions: "Have you seen him on a live video call? Can we look up his picture together?" Let her reach the conclusion herself.

A romance scam often continues after the first payment with new emergencies. Some victims are later contacted by "recovery agents" or "lawyers" offering to get the money back for a fee. That is usually the same group trying a second time. Genuine recovery happens through the police, EFCC and your bank, not through someone who found you online.

If intimate images or videos are being used to threaten you, stop all contact, do not pay, keep screenshots of the threats and the accounts, and report the account to the platform. Most platforms have a reporting option for non-consensual intimate images. Then report to the police cybercrime unit. Paying almost never ends the threats; it usually leads to bigger demands.

Ponzi schemes, fake investments and crypto traps
Explain how a Ponzi scheme pays old members with new members' money
Calculate why a promised return like 30% per month is unrealistic
Check whether an investment firm is registered with SEC Nigeria or licensed by the CBN
Recognise crypto and 'trading bot' traps

A **Ponzi scheme** promises high, steady returns but has no real business producing them. Early members are paid with money from newer members. As long as new money keeps flowing in, payouts continue and people trust it. When new money slows, the scheme freezes withdrawals, gives excuses, and collapses. Most members, especially later ones, lose their money.

Nigerians remember **MMM Nigeria**, which froze payouts in December 2016 after many people had joined, many of them recruited by friends and relatives. Since then, many other schemes have used the same pattern under new names: 'investment clubs', 'farm investment' plans, 'forex trading', 'crypto mining' and 'task-to-earn' apps.
Banknotes with wings flying away
In a Ponzi scheme the money flies from new members to old ones until it runs out.
Why Ponzi schemes must collapse
Founders paid first
Early members paid
Middle members waiting
Newest members lose all
Each layer needs a bigger layer below it, and no community has endless new members.
Run the numbers
A simple calculation shows why big monthly promises cannot be real. Suppose a scheme promises **30% profit every month**.
Worked example: what 30% a month really means
For example, Chioma is invited to put N100,000 into a scheme promising 30% monthly. Let us see what that would mean if the promise were real and profits were reinvested.
After 6 months: N100,000 x 1.3 x 1.3 x 1.3 x 1.3 x 1.3 x 1.3 = about N482,700.
After 12 months: about N2.33 million.
After 24 months: about N54 million from N100,000.
No legitimate business can grow money this way month after month. Even well-run banks and listed companies earn far less, and their returns go up and down.
The arithmetic proves the promise is impossible. Chioma declines. A return that sounds too good to be true is the clearest red flag in investing.
Signs of an investment scam
**Guaranteed high returns** with 'no risk'. All real investment carries some risk.
**Pressure to recruit** others, with bonuses for bringing people in.
**Vague explanation** of how money is made: 'forex', 'arbitrage', 'AI trading robot' with no audited details.
**Withdrawal problems:** delays, 'system upgrades', new fees to release your money, or a minimum you must reach first.
**Not registered** with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Nigeria, or claiming registration you cannot confirm.
**Payments to personal accounts** or crypto wallets rather than a regulated company account.
How to check a company
Look for the company on the **SEC Nigeria** website (sec.gov.ng). SEC registers capital market operators and publishes warnings about unregistered schemes.
For banks, microfinance banks and payment companies, check that they are licensed by the **Central Bank of Nigeria** on cbn.gov.ng.
A **CAC** registration only means a business name or company exists. It does **not** mean the company is allowed to take investments from the public.
Search the company name with 'SEC warning', 'scam' or 'withdrawal' to see others' experiences.
Ask for audited accounts and a written agreement. If they cannot give them, walk away.
Crypto and trading traps

Common versions include fake trading platforms that show your 'profit' growing on screen but never let you withdraw, 'account managers' on Telegram who trade for you, and fake crypto investment groups. If someone you met online offers to teach you trading and asks you to deposit on a platform they choose, treat it as a scam.

Why people stay in too long

Many people in a scheme see their 'balance' grow on the app dashboard and feel rich. But a number on a screen is not money in your bank account. The operators control that screen and can show any figure. Some people also get paid once or twice, which makes them trust the scheme and put in more, or bring relatives. That early payout is part of the trick: it is paid from newer members' money to build confidence.

If you are already in a scheme that has started delaying payments, do not put in more money to 'unlock' what is owed. Keep records and report it, as Module 4 explains. Keep a list of every payment you made, the dates, the account names and numbers you paid into, and screenshots of the app and group chats. Investigators need this trail, and it also helps you see clearly how much you have actually put in versus taken out.

This lesson covers three scams that grow quickly because they hit everyday needs: **work**, **shopping** and the **phone number** that protects your bank account.
A person looking at job offer cards on a screen
Real employers pay you; fake ones ask you to pay them.
Job scams

Fake job offers come through WhatsApp, Telegram, SMS, Facebook and fake recruitment websites. Common versions: 'like YouTube videos and earn N10,000 a day' task jobs; overseas jobs with visa 'processing'; government recruitment requiring a 'form fee'; and 'data entry from home' jobs that need a 'starter kit'. Some task jobs pay small amounts at first, then ask you to 'deposit' to unlock bigger tasks.
**You are asked to pay**: registration, training, medical test, uniform, visa or 'processing' fees. Real employers do not charge you to get a job.
**No real interview**, or an interview only by chat.
**Salary far above normal** for little work.
**Personal email or WhatsApp only**, with no verifiable company address or website.
**They ask early for BVN, bank login, or copies of your ID** 'for payroll' before any real offer letter.

If you are unsure, search the company's official website for its careers page, or call its office using a number from the official site. Many large companies post warnings that they never charge applicants.
Fake online shops

Fake vendors on Instagram, Facebook Marketplace, TikTok and WhatsApp post attractive prices, collect payment, then block you, or send something completely different. Some create fake pages that copy a real brand's name and photos.
Prefer **pay on delivery** or inspect-before-pay for first purchases from a new vendor.
Check the page age, comments and tagged customer posts. Be careful: followers and comments can be bought.
Ask for a live video of the actual item with today's date written on paper beside it.
Be wary when the account name you are paying does not match the business name.
For large purchases, use platforms with buyer protection or meet in a safe public place.
If the price is far below the market, assume it is fake.

Also watch for fake 'delivery' messages. A text says your parcel is waiting and asks you to click a link to pay a small redelivery fee. The page then collects your card details. If you are expecting a delivery, contact the seller or the courier through the number you already have.
Worked example: checking a vendor before paying
For example, Zainab in Kano finds a page selling a blender at N28,000 when shops sell it for much more. The vendor says, "Pay now, only two left, delivery tomorrow."
She checks the page: created three weeks ago, comments are all short 'I got mine' messages from accounts with no photos.
She asks for pay on delivery. The vendor refuses: "Company policy."
The account name for payment is a different personal name.
She asks for a live video with today's date. The vendor sends a stock photo instead.
Four red flags. Zainab does not pay. She buys from a known shop instead and reports the page to the platform.
SIM swap fraud

Your phone number receives your bank OTPs and password reset codes. In a **SIM swap**, a criminal gets your number moved to a new SIM card that he controls, for example by pretending to be you at a network office or by using details stolen from you. Once he controls your number, he can receive your OTPs and reset your banking or WhatsApp logins.

Act fast: from another phone, call your **network provider** to report a possible SIM swap and ask them to block the number, then call your **bank** to freeze transfers and online access until you confirm. Do this before anything else.

SIM swap fraud often comes after another scam. A criminal first collects your details through a fake form, a fake 'BVN update' call or a stolen phone. Then he uses them to request a replacement SIM. This is why protecting your NIN, BVN and date of birth matters even though they are not passwords: together they help a criminal pretend to be you.

To reduce your risk: protect your NIN and BVN, never post photos of your SIM pack or ID card, set a PIN on your SIM card in your phone settings, and add a PIN or two-step verification to WhatsApp (Settings, Account, Two-step verification). Ask your bank whether you can use a hardware token or app authenticator in addition to SMS.
Real employers never ask you to pay to get a job.
For new online vendors, insist on pay on delivery or a dated live video.

Sudden loss of service on only your line can mean a SIM swap. Speed matters, so contact the network and bank right away.

Pay, since medicals are normal

Decline: genuine employers do not charge applicants fees
Send your BVN instead of money

Protecting yourself, your money and your people

Build the habits and settings that stop most scams before they start: verifying through your own channels, locking down your phone, cards and accounts, and protecting your family, customers and community.
Verification habits: check through a channel you choose
Apply the 'own channel' rule to calls, messages and links
Verify a bank, network, employer or relative in under five minutes
Recognise phishing links and fake websites
Use a family code word for emergency requests

The single most powerful habit in this course is this: **never verify a message using the contact details inside the message**. If a text says "call this number to confirm", that number belongs to the scammer. If a link says "log in here", that page belongs to the scammer. Verification only works when you choose the channel yourself.

Verification means checking through a source you found, not one the message gave you.

Spotting fake links and websites
Phishing pages copy logos, colours and wording perfectly, so judging by looks is not enough. Still, some clues help:
**Check the web address**, not the page design. Look for small misspellings, extra words or unusual endings, for example a bank name followed by '-update' or '-verify' and then an unfamiliar domain.
**Shortened links** (such as bit.ly) hide where they really go.
**Pages that ask for everything at once**: account number, BVN, card number, PIN and OTP. No real bank page asks for your PIN in a web form.
**A padlock icon** only means the connection is encrypted. Scam sites can have padlocks too, so it is not proof of safety.
Bookmark, don't click

Install your bank's app from the official Google Play Store or Apple App Store, checking the publisher name. For websites you use often, type the address once and save it as a bookmark. Then always use the bookmark, never links in messages.
The family code word

Emergency scams say a loved one has been arrested, injured or kidnapped and needs money now. Voices can even be imitated with software today. A **family code word** solves this. Agree a simple word or phrase only your family knows, something not on social media. Anyone calling about an emergency must say it. If they cannot, you hang up and call your relative directly.
Worked example: verifying an emergency call

For example, Mama Tolu, 64, in Ilorin receives a call from an unknown number. A young man cries, "Mummy, it's me, I've had an accident, the police are holding me. Please send N120,000 to this officer's account now."
She remembers the family rule and asks, "What is our word?" The caller says, "Mummy, there's no time for that!"
She says she will call back and hangs up.
She calls Tolu's normal number. He answers from his office, safe.
She saves the scam number, blocks it and tells her church women's group about the call.
No money lost. The code word took ten seconds and stopped a N120,000 loss.

Stop. Do not click, reply or call back the number in the message.
Find the real contact yourself: card, SIM pack, official app, website you type in, or a relative's saved number.
Ask a simple question: "Did you contact me about this?"
If they say no, block and report the sender. If yes, continue through the official channel only.
Tell one trusted person what happened, even if it was nothing.
Verifying people and businesses you meet online

For a new business contact, a landlord advertising a house online, or an agent selling land, ask for things that are hard to fake: a physical address you can visit, a CAC registration number you can search on the CAC public search portal, and references from people you can call yourself. For property, never pay an 'inspection' or 'reservation' fee before seeing the place in person with someone you trust. A CAC search confirms a business is registered; it does not prove the person in front of you is honest, so combine it with other checks.

Most genuine organisations are glad when you verify. Scammers are the only ones who object. If you ever feel awkward asking, remember that a bank officer would far rather take your call than handle your fraud report.

Even careful people make payments every day. The goal is not to avoid digital money, which is convenient and widely used, but to set up your phone, cards and habits so that one mistake does not empty your account.
A person making a payment on a mobile phone

Lock down your phone and banking apps
**Screen lock:** use a PIN of at least six digits, a pattern that is not a simple shape, or fingerprint or face unlock. A phone with no lock is an open purse.
**Banking app PIN and transaction PIN:** choose numbers that are not your birthday, phone number or 1234. Use different PINs for your card and your app.
**Do not save PINs** in your phone notes or write them on your card.
**Update your phone and apps** when updates are offered. Updates fix security holes.
**Install apps only from Google Play Store or Apple App Store.** Never install an app because a caller told you to.
Set limits and alerts

Most Nigerian banks let you control how much can leave your account in a day through the app or by visiting the branch. A lower daily limit means that if a criminal gets access, he can take less. You can raise it temporarily when you need to make a big payment. Turn on SMS or app notifications for every debit so that you know immediately if something moves. Many banks also let you **freeze or block your card** in the app with one tap.

Collect your receipt and the card. Card swapping, where someone hands back a similar-looking card, is a known trick.

Checking money before you release goods
Worked example: a market shop's payment routine
For example, Esther sells foodstuff at a market in Jos. Her weekend sales include many transfers of N5,000 to N60,000.
She uses a POS or merchant app that shows incoming payments on its own screen, and she checks that screen, not customers' phones.
For transfers to her bank account, she checks her balance in the bank app before handing over goods worth more than N10,000.
When the network is slow, she politely asks customers to wait or to leave goods until payment shows.
At the end of the day she compares her written sales list with credits in her app.
On Saturday, a customer's transfer of N45,000 does not arrive. Esther keeps the goods, and the customer returns two hours later with cash.
In one month Esther has no losses from fake alerts. Her routine costs a few minutes and protects her profits.
Public Wi-Fi and shared phones
Avoid banking on public Wi-Fi or on someone else's phone. If you must log in on a shared device, log out fully afterwards and never let the browser save your password.

Plan this before it happens. If your card is lost, freeze it in the app or call your bank immediately. Then call your network to block the SIM and request a replacement through their official process. Change your email password from another device. The faster you act, the less time a thief has.

Create strong, different passwords and store them safely

Decide what personal information to keep private

Your email, WhatsApp and Facebook accounts are not just social tools. Your email can reset passwords for other accounts. Your WhatsApp can be used to message all your contacts asking for money in your name. Protecting these accounts protects your money and your friends.

Passwords that work

A strong password is **long and unique**. Length matters more than strange symbols. A good method is a **passphrase**: three or four unrelated words joined together, with a number, for example 'MangoBlueTaxi47Radio'. Do not use this example, create your own. Use a different password for your email than for anything else, because if your email is taken, everything linked to it can be reset.
Do not use your name, children's names, birthdays or phone number.
Do not reuse the same password across sites. When one site is leaked, criminals try it everywhere.
Store passwords in a password manager, such as the one built into Google or Apple accounts, or in a notebook kept safely at home, not in your phone notes.
Two-step verification

**Two-step verification** (also called two-factor authentication or 2FA) asks for a second proof, such as a code or a PIN, in addition to your password. Even if someone steals your password, they still cannot get in without the second step.

The WhatsApp code trick

A common trick: a friend's hacked account messages you, "I sent you a 6-digit code by mistake, please send it to me." That code is WhatsApp's registration code for **your** number. Sharing it hands over your WhatsApp. Never share any code that arrives by SMS.

Worked example: recovering a hacked WhatsApp
For example, Ifeoma's friends start calling to say 'she' has asked them for N20,000. She realises her WhatsApp has been taken over after she shared a code.
She reinstalls or opens WhatsApp on her phone and registers her number again. She receives a new SMS code and enters it. This logs the criminal out.
If WhatsApp asks for a two-step PIN she never set, the criminal has set one. She waits for the reset option WhatsApp offers and keeps trying to register her own number.
She posts a status and sends a broadcast message: 'My WhatsApp was hacked. Do not send any money in my name.'
She turns on two-step verification with her own PIN and adds an email.
She checks Linked Devices in WhatsApp settings and logs out any device she does not recognise.
Ifeoma regains her account the same day. Because she warned her contacts quickly, no one sends money.

Warning without panic

Many 'scam alerts' on WhatsApp are themselves false or exaggerated. Before forwarding, ask: Who wrote this? Does it come from an official account? Does it tell people a useful action? If you cannot check it, do not forward it, or say clearly that it is unverified. A good warning is short, accurate and practical.
The three-line warning
Use this pattern for every alert you share: 1. What happened. 2. The red flag. 3. What to do. People remember short, practical messages far better than long ones with lots of capital letters.

Children and teenagers are also targets, through gaming chats, fake giveaways and social media. Talk with them about never sharing passwords, never paying to 'unlock' prizes, and telling you if anyone online asks for photos or secrets. Make it clear they will not be punished for telling you.

People who feel supported report quickly, and quick reports give the best chance of recovery.

If a copycat page has taken money from your customers in your name, post a clear notice on your genuine pages, report the fake page to the platform, and encourage affected customers to report to their banks and the police. Keep a record of the fake page's name, link and account numbers it used.

If you realise you have been scammed, the next hour matters more than anything else. Money moved by transfer can be passed on to other accounts quickly. Reporting fast gives the banks the best chance to trace or hold it. Shame and shock make people freeze or wait until morning. Do not wait. Act now, and feel your feelings later.

Doing these steps in order gives the best chance of stopping money and protecting others.
Step 1: Call your bank immediately

Use the number on the back of your ATM card, in the official app, or go to the nearest branch. Tell them clearly: "I have been defrauded. I need to report a fraudulent transaction." Then ask for these specific actions:
**Block or freeze** your card, mobile banking and internet banking so no more money leaves.
**Contact the receiving bank** about the account you paid into, as quickly as possible, so that it can act on any money still in that account.
**Log a formal complaint** and give you a **complaint or reference number**. Write it down.
**Tell you what they need from you**: often a written statement, the transaction details and a police report.
Be honest about what happened
Tell the bank the full truth, including if you shared your OTP or PIN. Hiding it slows the investigation. Banks see these cases every day.
Step 2: Secure your accounts and SIM
Change your banking app password and PIN from your own phone, once the bank has confirmed it is safe to do so.
If you installed any app a scammer told you to install, especially screen-sharing or 'support' apps, uninstall it and tell your bank.
If you shared a WhatsApp or email code, recover those accounts and turn on two-step verification.
If your line went dead or you suspect a SIM swap, call your network provider to block the SIM and get a replacement through their official process.
Change the password on your email account, as it can reset other accounts.
Step 3: Collect evidence

Before you delete anything or block the scammer, save everything. Evidence helps the bank, the police and the EFCC. Take screenshots of chats and profiles, note phone numbers, account names and account numbers you paid into, dates and amounts of every transfer, and any website addresses. Download your bank statement showing the transactions. Keep all of it in one folder on your phone and, if possible, also on paper.
Worked example: Kemi's first hour
For example, Kemi, a hairdresser in Lagos, realises at 7:10 pm that she has been tricked into reading out an OTP, and N95,000 has left her account in two transfers.
7:12 pm: she calls her bank's official number from her ATM card, reports fraud, and asks them to block her mobile banking and card and to contact the receiving banks.
7:25 pm: the bank gives her a complaint reference number. She writes it on paper with the time.
7:30 pm: she screenshots the call log, the SMS OTP messages and the debit alerts, and notes both account numbers the money went to.
7:45 pm: she submits a report on the NPF National Cybercrime Centre website and plans to visit her local police station in the morning for a written report.
8:00 pm: she tells her sister, who helps her change her email password and stays with her.

Within the hour Kemi has stopped further losses and started the official process. Whether the money can be recovered depends on how much is still in the receiving accounts, but she has given herself the best possible chance.
Step 4 and 5: Report and warn

Next, report to the police and, for financial fraud, the EFCC, as the next lesson explains in detail. Then warn the people around you. If your WhatsApp or social media was used, send a message to your contacts saying not to send money in your name. If the scam came through a group, post a short warning there so others do not fall for the same trick tonight.
Beware the recovery scam

After a loss, you may be contacted by people claiming they can get your money back: 'hackers', 'recovery agents', 'lawyers', even people pretending to be from EFCC or a bank. They ask for an upfront fee. This is almost always a second scam, sometimes run by the same people. Genuine agencies do not charge victims to investigate. Only deal with your bank, the police and the EFCC through channels you found yourself.
Never pay to get your money back
Any offer to recover your money in exchange for a fee, especially from someone who found you online, should be treated as a scam.

At the police station, bring your evidence printed or on your phone, a means of identification, and your bank's reference number. Writing a clear report
Investigators handle many cases. A clear, complete report gets attention faster. Use this structure:
**Your details:** full name, phone number, address, bank and account number.
**What happened, in time order:** dates and times, how they contacted you, what they said, what you did.
**The money trail:** every amount, date, time, receiving account name, account number and bank.
**The scammer's details:** phone numbers, social media profile links, website addresses, names used.
**Evidence attached:** screenshots, bank statement, call logs.

Attached: screenshots of the page, the chat, my transfer receipt and my bank statement.

Musa submits it to his bank, the police and the EFCC website, and reports the Instagram page. Each agency has the same clear facts.
Following up

Keep a simple log of who you spoke to, when, and what they said. Follow up politely by phone or in writing. If your bank does not resolve a complaint, you can escalate to the **Central Bank of Nigeria's consumer protection** channels, which are listed on cbn.gov.ng. Have your bank's reference number ready, because the CBN usually expects you to have complained to the bank first.
Be realistic

Not every case ends with money returned. Reporting still matters: it can freeze accounts before more victims pay, it helps investigators connect cases, and in some cases it leads to recovery and prosecution.

When you report a scam number or page, you also protect others. Report scam SMS and calls to your network, and use the platform's Report option on fake profiles. On WhatsApp, open the chat, tap the contact name and choose Report. Reporting several times from different users makes action more likely.
What not to do
Do not confront or threaten the scammer. It can warn him to move money faster.
Do not pay anyone, including people claiming to be officials, to 'speed up' your case.
Do not post your account number, BVN or full bank statement publicly while asking for help.
Finally, keep copies of everything you submit. If you change phones, back up your evidence folder first. Some investigations take months, and you may be asked for the same documents again.

Emotional recovery and rebuilding after fraud
Recognise common feelings after being scammed
Separate self-blame from responsibility
Use practical steps to rebuild finances and confidence
Know when to seek extra support

Being scammed can hurt as much as a burglary or a betrayal, sometimes more. You lose money, and you may also lose trust in yourself and others. Many victims say the shame was harder than the money. This lesson is about recovering well, so that one bad experience does not shape the rest of your life.
Two people hugging
Support from people you trust speeds recovery after fraud.
Common feelings
**Shock and disbelief:** 'This can't be happening.'
**Shame and embarrassment:** 'How could I fall for this?'
**Anger:** at the scammer, at the bank, at yourself.
**Fear and anxiety:** jumping at every phone call or message.
**Sadness and grief:** especially after romance scams, where you also lose a relationship that felt real.
**Worry about money:** rent, school fees, business stock.
All of these are normal reactions. They usually ease with time, support and action.
The recovery cycle
Accept what happened
Take practical action
Talk to trusted people
Rebuild routines
Regain confidence
Recovery is not a straight line; you may go round this cycle more than once.
Self-blame versus responsibility

**Self-blame** says, 'I am stupid, I deserve this.' It keeps you stuck and silent. **Responsibility** says, 'A criminal deceived me. I will report it, learn from it and protect myself.' It moves you forward. The scammer is responsible for the crime. You are responsible only for what you do next. Professional criminals spend all day practising these tricks. Being deceived by a professional is not a sign of weakness.
Practical steps to rebuild
**Write down the full picture:** how much you lost, what bills are due, and what money you still have.
**Talk to anyone you owe** early, such as a landlord, supplier or school, and explain honestly. Many will give time.
**Make a short survival budget** for the next one to three months covering food, transport, rent and essentials.
**Avoid quick-fix loans** from unknown loan apps or 'investment' offers promising to replace your loss. Desperation makes people vulnerable to a second scam.
**Rebuild savings slowly**, for example through a trusted cooperative, a regulated bank savings account or a family esusu or ajo you know well.
Worked example: rebuilding after a Ponzi loss

For example, Bisi, a tailor in Osogbo, lost N400,000 in an investment scheme that froze withdrawals. Her monthly profit from sewing is about N120,000 (her own estimate) and her rent of N300,000 a year is due in four months.
She reports the scheme to the EFCC and SEC Nigeria with her payment records.
She tells her landlord early and asks to pay rent in two parts. He agrees.
She cuts non-essential spending and sets aside N40,000 a month in a separate savings account with no card.
After four months she has N160,000 saved: enough for the first part of the rent.
She joins a women's support group where others share their experiences and she no longer feels alone.
Bisi has not got her N400,000 back, but she has a plan, her rent is managed, and she has stopped blaming herself.
Rebuilding trust and confidence

Fear after a scam can make people avoid digital banking completely. That can bring its own problems, such as carrying too much cash. Instead, rebuild confidence step by step: use the security settings from Module 3, start with small transactions, and keep using the pause-and-verify habit. Every time you check something and stay safe, your confidence grows.
When to seek more help

If, weeks later, you still cannot sleep, eat, work or stop thinking about the loss, or if you feel hopeless, please talk to a doctor, a counsellor, a trusted religious leader or a mental health professional. Strong feelings after a loss are understandable, and help is available. You do not have to carry it alone.
Supporting someone else through it

If a friend or relative has been scammed, listen first. Avoid 'I told you so' and questions that begin with 'Why did you...'. Offer practical help: sit with her while she calls the bank, help her take screenshots, go with her to the police station. Check on her again a week later, when the first rush of support has faded.

Sharing your story, when you are ready, can also help. Many survivors say that warning others turned their pain into something useful. You do not have to share details you are not comfortable with. Even saying 'this happened to me, here is the red flag I missed' can protect someone else.

Keep your materials simple and cheap. Handwritten cards work as well as printed ones. If many members have basic phones, focus on calls, SMS and USSD rather than apps. If most have smartphones, include a short demonstration of WhatsApp two-step verification and Google Lens.

If your group wants to go further, you could invite a staff member from a local bank branch to speak about its official channels, or ask a police community relations officer how to report fraud locally. Always confirm such visits through official offices.

What a scam is
A scammer makes you open your own purse
You hand over money, codes or details yourself
The bank sees a payment you authorised
So recovery is slow, sometimes impossible
The best protection is a habit in your head
A pickpocket takes your purse. A scammer makes you open the purse yourself and give it away, often while saying thank you.
Because you made the transfer, typed the PIN or shared the code, the bank's records show a payment you authorised.
That is why getting the money back is slow, and sometimes impossible. It is not that the bank does not care.
So the best protection is not a lock on your door. It is a habit in your own head.
Three parts
Every scam needs these three parts
A believable reason to act: your BVN will be blocked, you won a promo, your son is in trouble.
Act now, before you think or ask anyone. Do it in 10 minutes. Don't tell anyone.
Always the same few things: money, a code such as your PIN or OTP, or your personal details.
New scams appear every month. But underneath, they are built from the same three parts. Spot the parts, and you do not need to memorise every trick.
First, the story. A believable reason to act.
Second, the pressure. You must act now, before you think, and often keep it secret so nobody can warn you.
Third, the request. It is always money, a code, or your personal details.
A real offer survives you slowing down and checking. A scam cannot. That is why pressure is always in the package.
Worked example
Ngozi takes apart a promo SMS
For example, Ngozi, a fish seller in Port Harcourt, gets an SMS saying her line won a promo.
The prize promised
Processing fee to pay first
Real prizes never make the winner pay first.
Ngozi's SMS says: congrats, your line has won a promo. Send a processing fee within 2 hours. Do not share this message.
The story is a 250,000 naira prize. The pressure is 2 hours, and secrecy. The request is a 5,000 naira fee to a personal account.
She never entered a promo. She calls her network on the official number from her SIM pack, not a number in the SMS. There is no promo. She deletes it, and warns her women's group.
Know the levers
Six feelings scammers use
Fear: your account will be blocked today
Greed or hope: double your money in 30 days
Urgency: offer closes in 15 minutes
Authority: this is EFCC, or your bank
Love and trust, or shame and secrecy
Scams work on feelings, not on lack of intelligence. Doctors, bankers and pastors have lost money too. Fear is the first lever.
Then greed or hope.
Urgency leaves no time to think.
Authority uses our respect for officials.
And love, or shame: don't tell your husband, he won't understand. Most scams combine two or three of these.
The cool-down rule saved Halima
Strong feeling plus money or codes: stop for at least 10 minutes.
Notice the feeling and name it
End the call: I will call the bank myself
Check through a number you found yourself
Tell one trusted person before paying
Halima, a teacher in Kaduna, got a call. He knew her name and her bank. Someone is withdrawing 180,000 naira right now, he said. Read me the code we just sent.
Authority, fear and urgency together. She noticed her fear.
She said, I will call the bank myself, and hung up.
She called the number on the back of her ATM card. Nobody from the bank had called. The code was for a transfer the scammer was trying to make.
Because she did not read it out, the transfer failed. Remember, a caller who knows your name and account number is not proven genuine. Account numbers are shared every day to receive payments.

Asks for a code or PIN?

A request for your PIN, password, OTP or card details is always a scam, because no genuine bank or office needs them from you.

Do not trust

A transfer screenshot

Your balance in your bank app

The most powerful habit
Never verify using the message itself
The number in the message belongs to the scammer
The link in the message belongs to the scammer
Your bank: the number on your ATM card
Your network: the number on your SIM pack
If a text says call this number to confirm, that number belongs to the scammer.
If a link says log in here, that page belongs to the scammer. Verification only works when you choose the channel yourself.
For your bank, use the number on the back of your ATM card, or the official app you installed yourself.
For your network, use the number on your SIM pack. For government, type the official address ending in dot gov dot n g yourself.
And remember, a padlock icon only means the connection is encrypted. Scam sites can have one too.
Worked example
Mama Tolu and the family code word
No code word? Hang up and call your relative directly.
Agree a secret family word, not on social media
Emergency caller? Ask: what is our word?
No word? Say you will call back, and hang up
Call your relative's normal number
Emergency scams say a loved one is arrested or injured. Voices can even be imitated with software today. So agree a simple family code word.
Mama Tolu, 64, in Ilorin got a call. A young man cried, Mummy, I've had an accident, send 120,000 naira to this officer's account now. She asked, what is our word?
He said, Mummy, there's no time for that. So she said she would call back, and hung up.
She called Tolu's normal number. He was safe at his office. The code word took ten seconds and stopped a 120,000 naira loss.
Lock down your money
Screen lock: a PIN of at least six digits
Different PINs for card and app, not 1234
A lower daily transfer limit
Debit alerts on, and know the card freeze
Most savings in a separate account
A phone with no lock is an open purse. Use a PIN of at least six digits, or your fingerprint.
Use different PINs for your card and your app. Not your birthday, phone number or 1234. And never save PINs in your phone notes.
Set a lower daily transfer limit. If a criminal gets in, he can take less. Raise it only when you need to.
Turn on alerts for every debit, and find the button that freezes your card in one tap.
Keep most of your money in a second account with no card, away from daily risk.

For example, Esther sells foodstuff at a market in Jos and takes many transfers.
Check app balance for goods over
Transfer that never arrived
No losses from fake alerts in one month.
Esther checks her merchant screen, never the customer's phone.
For goods worth more than 10,000 naira, she checks her balance in her bank app before handing them over.
One Saturday a 45,000 naira transfer did not arrive. She kept the goods. The customer came back two hours later with cash.
At POS and ATMs, keep your card in sight, cover the keypad, and refuse help from strangers.

No two-step verification

Your email can reset your other accounts. Your WhatsApp can be used to ask all your contacts for money.
A friend's hacked account says, I sent you a code by mistake, please send it. That is your own WhatsApp code. Sharing it hands over your account.

Use three or four unrelated words with a number. Turn on two-step verification. Ifeoma lost her WhatsApp after sharing a code. She registered her number again, warned her contacts, and set her own PIN. Nobody sent money.

To anyone. If someone asks, hang up.

Say you will never ask for PIN or OTP

Act now, feel later
The first hour after a scam
Do not wait until morning. Call your bank now.
Call your bank's official number
Secure your accounts, email and SIM

Money moved by transfer can be passed on quickly. Do not wait.
Step one. Call the number on your ATM card. Ask them to block your card and mobile banking, contact the receiving bank, and give you a reference number.
Step two. Uninstall any app a scammer told you to install. Change your email password, and if your line went dead, call your network to block the SIM.
Step three. Screenshot chats, numbers, account names, amounts and dates. Download your statement. Save it all in one folder.
Step four. Report to the police, and for financial fraud, the EFCC.
Step five. Warn your contacts, so nobody sends money in your name. Be honest with your bank, even if you shared your OTP. Hiding it slows the investigation.
